summary: The submitted hypotheses are overall plausible and grounded in known TXA physiology and CRASH trial results, and they already capture key moderators (injury pattern, shock physiology, time-to-treatment). They need refinement to (1) re-frame every hypothesis explicitly as a treatment-response interaction (which subgroup benefits more or less and why), (2) add conditional moderators (avoid monotone claims), (3) include concrete thresholds/strata where evidence exists (e.g., SBP <90 mmHg, time <1h/1-3h/>3h), (4) strengthen validation plans with explicit statistical tests and effect-size metrics (ARR, NNT), and (5) add important caveats about measurement error, power and confounding by differences in surgical timing. I provide per-feature reviews and a fully revised FeatureHypothesesSet that preserves all original hypotheses but rewrites them to be more precise, actionable, and testable.

issues.message: Original mechanism is plausible but framed as a prognostic statement rather than an explicit treatment-response interaction. Needs specification of which injury-type subgroup benefits more and why (with conditional moderators).

Suggested validation steps are reasonable but should be more concrete: specify statistical interaction tests, thresholds for subgroup definitions, adjustment covariates, and effect-size metrics (ARR, NNT).
Should emphasize coding heterogeneity, potential confounding by transport/time-to-surgery, and limited power for granular injury-type strata.

per_mechanism.comments: The mechanism that blunt polytrauma signals systemic hyperfibrinolysis and therefore greater TXA responsiveness is physiologically credible and consistent with observational data. However, the statement must be converted to an interaction claim (which subgroup benefits more) and must acknowledge conditional moderators (time-to-treatment, definitive haemorrhage control).
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Patients with blunt multisystem trauma (vs isolated penetrating injuries) derive larger absolute and likely larger relative benefit from TXA because blunt mechanisms more frequently produce diffuse bleeding and systemic fibrinolytic activation; the magnitude of benefit is greatest when TXA is given early (<3 hours, especially <1 hour) and when immediate operative control is not already achieved. Conversely, isolated penetrating injuries that are rapidly controlled surgically will show smaller incremental TXA benefit because definitive haemorrhage control, not antifibrinolysis, drives survival.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Define blunt vs penetrating and anatomic groups operationally (e.g., blunt polytrauma = ISS-based or multiple anatomic regions). Pre-specify comparisons and adjust for time-to-treatment and SBP. Report ARR/NNT per subgroup.

issues.message: The direction (low SBP -> greater benefit) is plausible but needs explicit thresholds and conditionality (e.g., SBP <90 mmHg; effect moderated by time and surgical control).
Validation should specify model form (interaction term in Cox/logistic model or CATE by SBP strata), covariates, and metrics (ARR, relative risk reduction).

per_mechanism.comments: Physiologic link between hypotension, trauma-induced coagulopathy/hyperfibrinolysis, and likely larger TXA effect is well supported. But SBP alone is noisy and effect is conditional on time-to-treatment and whether bleeding is surgically controlled quickly.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Hypotensive patients (operationally SBP <90 mmHg) derive greater absolute benefit from TXA compared with normotensive patients because hypovolaemic shock is associated with fibrinolytic activation; the relative benefit may also be larger, but this is moderated by time-to-treatment (largest benefit when treated within 3 hours, particularly <1 hour) and by whether immediate surgical haemostasis is achieved (if definitive haemorrhage control is immediate, incremental TXA benefit decreases).

per_feature.suggested_edits: Use SBP strata (e.g., <90, 90-110, >110 mmHg). Estimate treatment × SBP interaction controlling for age, GCS, injury type, time-to-treatment. Report ARR and NNT and test interaction significance (Wald test).

issues.message: Interpretation is broadly correct but needs mapping instructions (how to group ICC codes into clinically meaningful categories) and must specify interaction claims for each category (e.g., isolated severe TBI vs extracranial haemorrhage).
Validation should include mapping procedures and comparisons with CRASH-3 results; it should specify controlling for GCS and time.

per_mechanism.comments: CRASH-3 and physiologic reasoning support differential TXA responsiveness by injury category, especially head vs extracranial bleeding. The hypothesis should specify which ICC-derived groups show less benefit (severe isolated TBI with very low GCS) versus more benefit (extracranial exsanguinating injuries), and note conditional moderators (time, GCS).
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Specific ICC categories tag subgroups with distinct TXA responsiveness. For example, codes reflecting isolated severe TBI (especially with very low GCS) will show smaller or no mortality benefit from systemic TXA compared with codes indicating extracranial exsanguinating haemorrhage or combined head + extracranial bleeding. The magnitude of difference is moderated by time-to-treatment and baseline neurologic status: in intracranial bleeding, early (<3h) treatment in mild-moderate TBI may reduce head-injury death (as per CRASH-3), whereas in severe, unsurvivable TBI the systemic antifibrinolytic effect has limited impact on 28-day mortality.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Provide a reproducible mapping from ICC codes to groups (isolated severe TBI, major torso haemorrhage, combined injuries). Compare treatment effects to CRASH-3 head injury strata, adjust for GCS and time, and present subgroup-specific ARRs and interaction p-values.

issues.message: Time-sensitive effect is well established (CRASH-2), but exact cutpoints and generalisability need caution. The description should remain an interaction claim and include concrete strata and conditional moderators.
Validation should specify strata and analytic approach, and quantify effect size by stratum, adjusting for confounders and reporting ARR/NNT.

per_mechanism.comments: CRASH-2 provides strong trial evidence of a time-dependent TXA effect. The mechanism framing is sound; refinement should add strata (0-1h, 1-3h, >3h), acknowledge measurement error, and explicitly note interactions with injury type and haemorrhage control.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: TXA confers the largest absolute and relative mortality benefit when administered early: greatest within the first hour, still beneficial within 1-3 hours, and little or no benefit (possible harm) after ≈3 hours. This is because early inhibition of fibrinolysis prevents progression to fatal haemorrhage; the time effect is moderated by injury type (e.g., intracranial vs torso) and by whether definitive haemorrhage control is achieved quickly.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Estimate treatment × time strata interactions (0-1h, 1-3h, >3h), adjust for injury type, SBP, GCS. Present ARR and NNT by stratum and test trend across time. Include sensitivity analysis for misrecorded injury times.

issues.message: Original text suggests high HR -> less benefit, which is plausible but oversimplified. Need to reframe as conditional interaction (HR × SBP × time) and give operational thresholds for "very high" HR.
HR is nonspecific; must caution confounding by pain, drugs, neurogenic causes. Validation must control for these and examine mediation.

per_mechanism.comments: Marked tachycardia often accompanies major bleeding and can signify high bleeding volume and longer prehospital time, which could reduce incremental TXA effect if haemorrhage is uncontrolled. But HR is non-specific, and a better interpretation frames HR as a modifier only in combination with hypotension and delay.
per_mechanism.suggested_revision: Extremely high presenting heart rate (operationally HR ≥120 bpm) is associated with smaller TXA benefit when combined with hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) or long prehospital time (>1-3h), because this constellation likely indicates prolonged, high-volume bleeding where definitive haemostasis, not antifibrinolysis, determines outcome. Isolated moderate tachycardia without hypotension/time delay should not be taken as evidence of reduced TXA responsiveness.

per_feature.suggested_edits: Test HR strata (e.g., <90, 90-119, ≥120 bpm) interacting with TXA and include SBP and time as moderators (three-way interaction or stratified analyses). Control for confounders (beta-blocker use, neurogenic shock). Report effect sizes and mediation by transfusion volume.

revised.summary: Refined interaction-focused hypotheses: injury type, SBP, ICD-derived injury categories, delay to TXA, and heart rate modify the treatment effect of tranexamic acid (TXA) on 28-day/in-hospital mortality. Each hypothesis is framed as a testable treatment-response interaction with operational subgroup definitions, conditional moderators (most importantly time-to-treatment and whether definitive haemorrhage control occurred), concrete validation steps (statistical interaction tests, ARR/NNT reporting, mediation analyses), and explicit caveats about measurement error, confounding, and power.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Mechanism and anatomic injury type (e.g., blunt multisystem vs isolated penetrating; region: head, torso, extremity) capturing bleeding pattern and likelihood of systemic fibrinolysis.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Injury mechanism and distribution influence whether bleeding is diffuse/systemic (more likely to generate hyperfibrinolysis and benefit from systemic antifibrinolysis) or focal and surgically controllable (less incremental benefit from TXA).

mechanisms.description: Interaction claim: Patients with blunt multisystem trauma (operationally defined as involvement of ≥2 anatomic regions or ISS-based proxy) derive larger absolute and likely larger relative benefit from TXA compared with patients with isolated penetrating injuries because blunt trauma more often produces diffuse bleeding with systemic fibrinolysis that is amenable to antifibrinolysis. The magnitude of benefit is greatest when TXA is given early (<3 hours, particularly <1 hour) and when definitive operative haemostasis is not immediately performed; conversely, isolated penetrating injuries that undergo rapid surgical control will show smaller incremental TXA benefit because haemorrhage control (not antifibrinolysis) determines survival.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Prioritise TXA for blunt multisystem trauma and major torso contusions when treatment is early and immediate surgery is not already planned; expect smaller ARR and higher NNT in isolated penetrating wounds with rapid operative control.
validation_suggestions: Define groups: blunt multisystem (≥2 regions or ISS proxy) vs isolated penetrating. Pre-specify cutpoints and sample sizes.
Estimate treatment × injury-type interaction using adjusted regression/CATE models (include age, GCS, SBP, time-to-treatment).
Report subgroup-specific absolute risk reduction (ARR), relative risk reduction (RRR), and NNT with 95% CIs; test interaction (Wald or likelihood-ratio).
Mediation: if available, compare viscoelastic markers (TEG/ROTEM) or D-dimer prevalence across groups to assess mediation by hyperfibrinolysis.
Sensitivity: restrict to cases without immediate operative intervention (or adjust for time-to-surgery) to separate effect from definitive haemostasis.
caveats: Injury-type coding can be coarse; misclassification biases subgroup estimates.
Blunt vs penetrating is correlated with other factors (transport time, mechanism of prehospital care); residual confounding possible despite randomization being preserved for treatment assignment.
Power may be limited for granular anatomic subgroups; adjust analyses for multiplicity and present CIs.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Initial systolic blood pressure on presentation — a proxy for hemorrhagic shock severity and likelihood of fibrinolytic activation.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Hypotension increases the probability that bleeding has triggered trauma-induced coagulopathy and hyperfibrinolysis; TXA is mechanistically more likely to reduce bleeding deaths in these patients.

mechanisms.description: Interaction claim: Patients presenting with hypotension (operational threshold SBP <90 mmHg) gain larger absolute benefit from TXA than normotensive patients because hypotension is associated with fibrinolytic activation. The effect is conditional: the benefit is largest when hypotensive patients receive TXA early (<3h, especially <1h) and when definitive haemorrhage control has not yet been achieved. If hypotension co-occurs with immediate surgical control, the incremental benefit of TXA is attenuated.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Prioritize early TXA in patients with SBP <90 mmHg, especially when surgery is delayed; expect diminishing ARR in higher SBP strata and when operative control is immediate.
validation_suggestions: Use SBP strata (<90, 90-110, >110 mmHg) and fit treatment × SBP interaction in adjusted models (covariates: age, GCS, injury-type, time-to-treatment).
Report ARR, RRR, and NNT per SBP stratum and test interaction (Wald/likelihood-ratio).
Examine mediation by transfusion volume and viscoelastic markers if available.
Sensitivity: use prehospital SBP where recorded to reduce ED-resuscitation bias and perform analyses excluding patients receiving large prehospital fluids/vasopressors.
caveats: SBP is subject to measurement error and resuscitation effects; single measurements may misclassify shock.
SBP correlates with age, medications, and neurogenic shock — adjust for these confounders.
CRASH-2 subgroup evidence on SBP alone is limited; this remains a plausible but not definitive effect modifier.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Coded injury categories that can be mapped to clinical groups (e.g., isolated severe TBI, major torso haemorrhage, combined injuries) and reflect differing pathophysiology and time-course of bleeding.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Certain coded injuries — especially severe isolated intracranial haemorrhage — may not derive the same systemic TXA benefit as extracranial exsanguination; TXA effect varies by pathology and neurologic status.

mechanisms.description: Interaction claim: ICC-derived categories identifying isolated severe TBI (particularly with very low GCS) will show smaller or absent mortality benefit from systemic TXA relative to extracranial haemorrhage categories. Conversely, ICCs indicating major extracranial bleeding or combined head + torso bleeding are more likely to show preserved or greater TXA benefit. The magnitude depends on neurologic status (GCS) and timing — early TXA may reduce head-injury death in mild-moderate TBI (consistent with CRASH-3), but in unsurvivable severe TBI the effect on 28-day mortality is minimal.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Map ICC to clinically meaningful groups and expect differential ARRs: small/no ARR in unsurvivable isolated TBI, measurable ARR in extracranial haemorrhage groups and possibly in less-severe intracranial bleeding when treated early.
validation_suggestions: Create reproducible mapping from ICC codes to groups (isolated severe TBI vs major torso haemorrhage vs combined).
Fit treatment × ICC-group interactions adjusted for GCS, SBP, time-to-treatment; compare to CRASH-3 head-injury strata.
Report subgroup ARRs and interaction p-values; perform mediation analysis by bleed volume (imaging) if available.
caveats: ICC codes are administratively assigned and vary by site; mapping is imperfect.
Heterogeneity within ICC categories can produce average negative effects even when some subcodes benefit.
Separation of neurologic and extracranial causes of death can be challenging; cause-of-death misclassification may bias subgroup results.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Elapsed time (minutes/hours) between injury and TXA administration; a time-sensitive determinant of antifibrinolytic efficacy.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: TXA's mechanism (inhibition of fibrinolysis) is most effective early in the bleeding course; delay allows progression to phases less amenable to antifibrinolysis.

mechanisms.description: Interaction claim: The mortality reduction from TXA is time-dependent: largest benefit when administered within the first hour, still beneficial within 1-3 hours, and little or no benefit (possible attenuation or harm) beyond ~3 hours. This time effect is moderated by injury type and physiological status (e.g., intracranial bleeding may have a different time-sensitivity), and by whether definitive haemorrhage control occurs rapidly.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Expect greatest ARR and lowest NNT in 0-1h group, measurable benefit in 1-3h, and little/no benefit >3h; policy implication is to prioritize very early TXA administration in suspected bleeding.
validation_suggestions: Pre-specify time strata (0-1h, 1-3h, >3h). Fit interaction models adjusted for injury-type, SBP, GCS. Report ARRs, RRRs, NNTs per stratum and test for trend.
Perform sensitivity analyses for misrecorded injury times and assess robustness using prehospital vs ED-recorded times.
Mediation: estimate how much of time-dependent benefit is mediated by transfusion volume or fibrinolysis markers if available.
caveats: Time-of-injury is often imprecise, particularly in prehospital settings; misclassification can bias estimates toward the null.
Time interacts with injury type and care pathway; a single time effect is an oversimplification unless conditioned on these factors.
CRASH-2 provides strong support for time-dependence, but subgroup analyses may be underpowered for fine-grained strata.

feature_hypotheses.clinical_interpretation: Initial heart rate on presentation, a nonspecific physiological marker reflecting bleeding, pain, anxiety, neurogenic influence, or medications.
feature_hypotheses.why_important: Marked tachycardia may flag high-volume/prolonged bleeding and physiologic exhaustion, contexts in which the incremental benefit of TXA could be reduced because definitive haemorrhage control and resuscitation determine survival.

mechanisms.description: Interaction claim: Extremely high HR (e.g., ≥120 bpm) in combination with hypotension (SBP <90 mmHg) or long prehospital delay predicts a smaller TXA treatment effect because this constellation suggests prolonged, high-volume hemorrhage where antifibrinolysis alone is insufficient. By contrast, moderate tachycardia without hypotension or delay should not be interpreted as reducing TXA responsiveness.

feature_hypotheses.subgroup_implications: Anticipate reduced ARR among patients with HR ≥120 bpm plus SBP <90 mmHg or long (>1-3h) delay; do not use HR alone to withhold TXA without considering SBP and time.
validation_suggestions: Define HR strata (<90, 90-119, ≥120 bpm) and fit treatment × HR interactions with SBP and time as moderators (three-way tests or stratified analyses).
Adjust for confounders (beta-blocker use, neurogenic injury, sepsis) and examine mediation by transfusion requirements and timing of surgery.
Sensitivity: repeat analyses excluding patients with non-bleeding causes of tachycardia where possible.
caveats: HR is highly non-specific; observed interactions may reflect confounding by other indicators of illness severity.
Cutpoints for HR are arbitrary and should be validated; continuous analyses with splines may be preferable if sample size allows.
Power to detect three-way interactions (HR × SBP × time) may be limited; interpret negative findings cautiously.

revised.cross_feature_patterns: Coherent pattern: features that indicate active systemic bleeding and recent injury (blunt multisystem trauma, low SBP, short time-to-treatment) predict larger TXA benefit; features that indicate either focal injuries not responsive to systemic antifibrinolysis (specific ICC categories for severe isolated TBI) or prolonged/exhausted physiology (very high HR with hypotension and long delay) predict attenuated benefit. Important conditionalities: time-to-treatment consistently moderates other interactions (SBP, injury type, ICC), and analyses should report absolute effect sizes (ARR, NNT) and test interaction terms while adjusting for confounders (age, GCS, operative timing). Validation should prioritize pre-specified strata, mediation by fibrinolysis markers/transfusion, and sensitivity to measurement error.
